chunk_findings.detail:
The new header promotion still promotes a table-like data row to a header whenever it contains a cell named `id` or `title` and the next line is delimiter-like, even when the scanner is already inside a table. Given:

```markdown
| id | title |
| --- | --- |
| T-1 | id |
| --- | --- |
| T-2 | Bar |
```

the second `| --- | --- |` is a data row of the first table under GFM (a visual separator), but at `| T-1 | id |` `_table_columns` yields a mapping containing `id`, `_table_delim` accepts the next line, and the scanner replaces the real column map with `{"id": 1}` and skips the separator. The task `T-1` is not emitted, and `T-2` is then parsed with the wrong column map (no title column) and is also dropped. The previous fix only prevented the misclassification when no delimiter-like row follows; with a delimiter-like data row the scanner still silently loses tasks.

chunk_findings.detail: `_one_run` discards any run whose final shell exit status is 126 or 127. chunk_findings.detail: Treating `sel.neutral` (import-order/format-only) as behaviour-neutral is unsound for a hub module in Python: import order can change module initialization side effects, circular-import resolution, and global registration. Given a hub module whose lint-only diff only swaps two imports, e.g. `import ddflow.plugins` before `import ddflow.config` changed to the reverse, `behaviour_neutral` can mark the change neutral, `ci_scope` returns a selected plan, and tests that exercise behavior affected by the registration order but do not directly import the hub are not run; the gate can pass while the full suite would fail.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ci_scope.py:182

chunk_findings.detail:
`_signature` compares top-level imports and top-level non-import statements as two independent sorted/unsorted lists, so it ignores the relative order of imports and other module-level code. Given base:
```python
import os
__all__ = [os.name]
```
changed to:
```python
__all__ = [os.name]
import os
```
`imports` is still one `Import(os)` signature and `rest` is the same `__all__` assignment dump, so `_signature` is equal and `behaviour_neutral` returns `True`. The changed module raises `NameError` when imported, but a hub touched by this change is treated as lint-only and the whole-suite fallback is suppressed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_signature (lines 113-120)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_signature` sorts all top-level import statements, treating import order as unobservable. Python import order can be observable, e.g. star imports with overlapping names. Given base:
```python
from a import *
from b import *
```
changed to:
```python
from b import *
from a import *
```
If `a` and `b` both define `f`, the module’s final `f` binding changes. The two signatures are identical because the import statements are sorted, so `behaviour_neutral` returns `True` and the hub whole-suite fallback is skipped even though test behavior can change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_signature (lines 113-114)

chunk_findings.detail: The new `neutral` path is built on the false premise, stated in the added comment, that an import-order-only diff “cannot change any test outcome.” Python import statements have observable side effects and order can change behavior: modules may register plugins, mutate globals or `sys.modules`, set environment variables, or resolve circular imports differently depending on which import executes first. For example, if a hub changes from `import side_effect_first; import depends_on_side_effect` to `import depends_on_side_effect; import side_effect_first`, the diff is only import ordering, so `_hub_answer` can set `sel.neutral=True` and suppress the hub whole-suite fallback. A test that exercises the affected behavior indirectly, especially beyond the selected hop budget or under a different test/import order, can fail, but the ci/unit_tests gate will no longer run the whole suite that would catch it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:Selected.neutral

chunk_findings.detail:
The new logic treats an import-order-only change to a hub as “behaviour-neutral”, but Python import order is observable when imported modules have side effects or circular imports. For example, with `pkg/hub.py` base `from pkg import other
from pkg import mod
` and branch `from pkg import mod
from pkg import other
`, where `pkg/mod.py` is `from pkg import other
Y = 1` and `pkg/other.py` is `from pkg import mod
X = mod.Y`, the base import succeeds but the branch raises `AttributeError` at import time. The added test asserts `"behaviour-neutral" in res.scope["why"]` for such a reorder, so the CI gate can classify a real behavioural change as lint-only and limit the unit_tests gate to the direct hub importers, missing failures in tests affected through conftest, indirect imports, or global import side effects.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/testselect.py:_hub_answer / behaviour_neutral

chunk_findings.detail:
`_signature` compares `ast.dump(mod, include_attributes=False)`, so changes that only move source positions are treated as neutral. That is not always behaviour-neutral for pytest, because traceback line numbers are observable. Given a hub `h.py` whose base body is:

```python
def f():
    raise ValueError("boom")
```

and a test that asserts `excinfo.reprcrash.lineno == 2` (or `excinfo.traceback[-1].lineno == 2`), a whitespace-only change inserting a blank line before the `raise` produces the same AST dump, so `behaviour_neutral` returns `True` and `ci_scope` takes the neutral path instead of the hub whole-suite fallback. The test now fails because the exception line number is 3. If that test would only have been covered by the hub whole-suite fallback, the selected plan misses a real failure; the claim that whitespace-only changes cannot be observed by pytest is false.

chunk_findings.detail: `_signature` treats equality of `ast.dump(mod, include_attributes=False)` as proof that the change differs only by whitespace/comments and cannot affect a test, but stripping AST attributes also strips line/column positions and AST equality ignores non-whitespace source differences such as redundant parentheses, line continuations, adjacent string-literal concatenation, shebang/encoding comments, and comment text. Given a hub `h.py` containing `raise ValueError("boom")` on line 1, changing it by inserting one blank line before the raise (or changing `x = (1)` to `x = 1`) produces the same signature, so `behaviour_neutral` returns `True` and `_hub_answer` clears the hub whole-suite fallback. A test such as `tests/test_tracebacks.py` that does not import `h.py` but either reads `h.py` and asserts `lines[0] == 'raise ValueError("boom")'` or runs it in a subprocess and asserts the traceback says `line 1` fails on the branch; because that test has no import/name relation to the hub, it is not in the selected paths, so `ci_scope` can return a selected plan and the gate passes while the full suite fails.

chunk_findings.detail: `behaviour_neutral` judges only changed `.py` files and returns `True` when every Python file is whitespace/comment-only, even when the change also contains non-Python files that can affect tests. For example, if `ddflow/services/hub.py` is comment-only but `ddflow/data/zzz.json` is also changed, `behaviour_neutral` still returns `True`, `_hub_answer` suppresses the hub whole-suite fallback, and `ci_scope` can return a selected plan whose `why` says the change is whitespace/comment-only. A test like `tests/test_feature.py` that reads `ddflow/data/zzz.json` and asserts a value from it, without importing the hub or naming the data file stem, fails because of the JSON change but is not selected by the Python import/name selection; the gate passes on the selected scope although the full suite fails.

chunk_findings.detail: The AST-only signature ignores blank lines and comments, and the new test at `tests/test_ci_selected_scope.py:117` makes that the rule for hubs: a branch that inserts a blank line and a comment is “behaviour-neutral” and CI runs only `tests/test_h1.py` and `tests/test_h2.py`. That is wrong. Add `tests/test_cli_traceback.py` that does not import `pkg.hub` but runs the CLI in a subprocess and asserts a traceback from code in `pkg.hub` contains `line 2`; the blank line in the branch shifts that traceback to `line 3`, so the test newly fails. Because the test does not import the hub, the selected pytest invocation expected by the new test omits it, so the gate can record a passing selected run while a real regression exists. The previous “full AST” fix only prevents import reordering from being neutral; it does not make position/comment-only changes safe.

chunk_findings.detail: `behaviour_neutral` assumes a change that only alters comments, blank lines, or whitespace cannot change any test outcome because `_signature` compares AST dumps with comments stripped. That assumption is false: a test can observe a module’s source text directly without importing it. Given a changed hub file `ddflow/services/hub.py` that deletes a comment `# REQUIRED`, and a test `tests/test_hub_markers.py` containing `assert "# REQUIRED" in (repo_root / "ddflow/services/hub.py").read_text()`, the AST signature is unchanged, so `neutral` is set and the whole-suite fallback is suppressed. The import-reach selection does not include this source-reading test, so the failing test is never run and the gate passes.

chunk_findings.detail: The change moves `recover` out of `ddflow/api/reporting/health.py` and adds a complexity baseline for the new `ddflow.api.reporting.recovery` module, but the manifest shows no modification to the complexity baseline for `ddflow.api.reporting.health`. The stated guard failure lists `doctor` CC27 in `health.py`, and `doctor` is neither moved nor simplified in this change. Running the architecture guard after this change will still evaluate `doctor` against the unchanged/missing health baseline, so the complexity ratchet remains red; if the old health baseline also contained an entry for the now-removed `recover`, that entry is stale as well. Thus the CI failure this task is meant to fix is not fully fixed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:doctor

chunk_findings.detail: The moved `recover` implementation still filters by `item` only after `L.sweep` has already been called with `apply=apply`. For example, if two expired leases/orphan worktrees exist (`A` and `B`) and the caller invokes `recover(repo, item="A", apply=True)`, `L.sweep(log, cfg, repo, apply=True)` is run over the whole repo first, so `B` is recovered/touched even though the caller scoped the operation to `A`; the subsequent list comprehension merely hides `B` from the returned `found` list. If no `A` result is present, the function can return `O.nothing(...)` (exit “nothing to recover”) even though it already applied recovery actions to unrelated items. The `--item` scoping should be passed to the side-effecting sweep, or the sweep must be restricted before applying.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/recovery.py:recover

chunk_findings.detail: In the non-`all`/non-`plan` branch, `L.sweep(log, cfg, repo, apply=apply)` is called before filtering by `item`, so `item` does not scope the side effect. For example, calling `recover(repo, item="foo", apply=True)` in a repo with an expired lease/orphan worktree for `bar` causes `L.sweep` to apply to `bar`, then the list comprehension drops `bar` because `r.item != "foo"`. If there is no `foo`, the function returns `O.nothing("recover", "Nothing to recover — no expired leases, no orphan worktrees.", ...)` even though `bar` was swept/applied; if there is also a `foo`, the outcome reports only `foo` while `bar` was mutated. The `all`/`plan` path filters `L.scan` before triage and `SR.apply`, indicating the intended behavior is that `item` scopes recovery actions.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/recovery.py:53

chunk_findings.detail: The change does not remove the services→surfaces dependency; it only hides it from the architecture guard. `importlib.import_module("ddflow.surfaces.cli")` is still a deferred cross-layer import executed at runtime, but it is no longer a `from ... import ...` statement that a static deferred-import/import-contract guard can reliably see. As a result, the guard can pass while `ddflow.services.docscheck_help` still reaches up into `ddflow.surfaces.cli`. If `ddflow.surfaces.cli` is later refactored (for example, `build_parser` is moved or the CLI module becomes importable only through the CLI entry point), the guard will not flag the service dependency and `ddflow docscheck help` will fail at runtime with `AttributeError`/`ImportError`. Conversely, if the guard does scan `importlib.import_module`, the violation remains and no baseline for `docscheck_help` is added, so the stated guard failure is not fixed either way.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docscheck_help.py:61

chunk_findings.detail: `record` logs the caller-supplied evidence over the ddflow-measured evidence: `evidence={**(measured or {}), **(evidence or {})}`. If a caller invokes `record(..., measured={"tree": "real-fingerprint", "diff_size": 12}, evidence={"tree": "forged"})`, the persisted event contains `evidence["tree"] == "forged"`, not the tree fingerprint ddflow measured. The docstring says `measured` is what ddflow determined itself and that both are recorded, but the merge order lets the caller clobber the audit-critical measured fields, so later consumers reading the logged evidence cannot trust the measured tree/diff values.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/hand_approve.py:record

chunk_findings.detail: The human-gate check is bypassable by the caller because `record` accepts `human: bool` and only refuses when `human` is false. For example, `record(log, cfg, item, "some-human-gate", "passed", evidence={"note": "ok"}, gates=gates, human=True)` records a passed outcome for a human gate. Since `record` is the service boundary and is reachable from surfaces, accepting a caller-controlled privilege flag means the boundary does not actually enforce that only `approve` can clear a human gate; any surface that forwards `human=True` can self-approve.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/hand_approve.py:record

chunk_findings.detail: The split preserves attribute access (`outcomes.record`/`outcomes.approve`) but silently changes the module in which the moved functions resolve their dependencies. `record` and `approve` now live in `hand_approve.py`, so their global lookups go through `hand_approve`, not `outcomes`. For example, an existing test or caller that does `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.services.gates.outcomes, "EventLog", FakeLog)` and then calls `outcomes.record(...)` will still call the real `EventLog`, because `hand_approve.record` looks up `EventLog` in `hand_approve`’s globals. Likewise, patching `outcomes.record` no longer affects `outcomes.approve` if `approve` calls `record` internally, because `approve` calls `hand_approve.record`. The change only aliases the function objects and does not re-export or shim the dependency globals, so the old monkeypatch seam is broken without any compatibility layer.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/outcomes.py (import of `hand_approve`)

chunk_findings.detail: The patch deletes the complexity ratchet for `ddflow.services.gates.reviewers` even though the change contains no modification to `ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py` and the stated bug list does not mention a reviewers split or removal. The deleted file recorded `baseline = 1`, meaning the module had one D-or-worse function. Given that the module itself is unchanged, the architecture guard will now see one current violation with no baseline file (default 0) and fail, or, if the guard only iterates existing baseline files, it will silently stop checking that module and allow future complexity regressions. The baseline should have been retained, or the complex function should have been removed/refactored and the zero state demonstrated.

Given the current code still contains the deferred-import sites in that file, running the architecture guard after this change will still fail the deferred-import ratchet for `ddflow/surfaces/__init__.py`, so the intended CI-green housekeeping fix is incomplete.
chunk_findings.title: tests/guard_baselines/deferred_imports (missing `ddflow.surfaces`)

chunk_findings.detail: The split moves `recover` out of `ddflow/api/reporting/health.py` and adds a new complexity baseline for `ddflow.api.reporting.recovery`, but the manifest shows no update to `tests/guard_baselines/complexity_d_or_worse/ddflow.api.reporting.health.toml`. Since the stated baseline-red condition includes `recover` CC44 in `health.py`, the old health baseline entry for `recover` remains after the move. This leaves the health module’s ratchet authorizing a D-or-worse function named `recover` in `health.py` even though that function is now in `recovery.py`; a future regression that reintroduces a complex `recover` in `health.py` will be silently suppressed, and if the guard validates baseline entries against current findings, the health baseline also remains stale/red.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/health.py:recover

chunk_findings.detail: In the non-`all`/non-`plan` path, the side-effecting sweep runs before the `item` filter is applied. Given a repo with expired leases for items `A` and `B`, a call like `recover(repo, item="A", apply=True)` executes `L.sweep(..., apply=True)` over all leases, then discards the `B` result on line 53. `B`'s lease state is therefore changed silently while the outcome reports only `A` (`count == 1`, `found` contains only `A`). This contradicts the `item` filter used elsewhere in the same function: the `all`/`plan` path filters recoveries, dead runs, jobs and queue entries before triage/apply, so `item` should limit the applied side effects, not merely hide them after they have happened.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/recovery.py:53

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the deferred static import `from ..surfaces.cli import build_parser` with `importlib.import_module("ddflow.surfaces.cli").build_parser()`. This does not remove the forbidden `ddflow.services` -> `ddflow.surfaces` dependency; it only hides it from static import-contract analysis. Calling `_help_text` from a service-only import path still executes `import ddflow.surfaces.cli` at runtime, pulling the CLI layer into services, and if the CLI module is unavailable or only partially initialized (because the CLI imports services) the call fails, while the architecture guard can report clean because no literal `import` statement is present. The stated `import_contracts` fix is therefore bypassed rather than fixed.

chunk_findings.detail: The moved `recover` implementation still filters by `item` only after `L.sweep` has already been called with `apply=apply`. For example, if two expired leases/orphan worktrees exist (`A` and `B`) and the caller invokes `recover(repo, item="A", apply=True)`, `L.sweep(log, cfg, repo, apply=True)` is run over the whole repo first, so `B` is recovered/touched even though the caller scoped the operation to `A`; the subsequent list comprehension merely hides `B` from the returned `found` list. If no `A` result is present, the function can return `O.nothing(...)` (exit “nothing to recover”) even though it already applied recovery actions to unrelated items. The `--item` scoping should be passed to the side-effecting sweep, or the sweep must be restricted before applying.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/reporting/recovery.py:recover

chunk_findings.detail: In the non-`all`/non-`plan` branch, `L.sweep(log, cfg, repo, apply=apply)` is called before filtering by `item`, so `item` does not scope the side effect. For example, calling `recover(repo, item="foo", apply=True)` in a repo with an expired lease/orphan worktree for `bar` causes `L.sweep` to apply to `bar`, then the list comprehension drops `bar` because `r.item != "foo"`. If there is no `foo`, the function returns `O.nothing("recover", "Nothing to recover — no expired leases, no orphan worktrees.", ...)` even though `bar` was swept/applied; if there is also a `foo`, the outcome reports only `foo` while `bar` was mutated. The `all`/`plan` path filters `L.scan` before triage and `SR.apply`, indicating the intended behavior is that `item` scopes recovery actions.

chunk_findings.detail: `record` logs the caller-supplied evidence over the ddflow-measured evidence: `evidence={**(measured or {}), **(evidence or {})}`. chunk_findings.detail: The human-gate check is bypassable by the caller because `record` accepts `human: bool` and only refuses when `human` is false. chunk_findings.detail: The `limit` value is accepted as any integer, but `text` treats it as a slice bound. With `args={"limit": -1}` and a wave containing one item, `report` stores `limit=-1`, then `text` evaluates `ids[:-1]`, which returns an empty list and prints `... 1 more (--limit 0 lists all)`. A negative limit therefore produces incorrect truncation instead of either being rejected or treated as “no limit” like `0`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/waves.py:text

chunk_findings.detail: `_STAMPING` is a process-wide boolean, not a per-command/thread/context-local guard. `keep_stamped` disables itself whenever `_STAMPING` is true (`on = not _STAMPING and bool(cfg.waves.auto_stamp)`), and it sets `_STAMPING = True` for the duration of `waves.restamp(...)`. In an MCP server or any threaded/async host that can have two ddflow commands in flight, a restamp for command A will make an unrelated command B take the `if not on: yield; return` path. B can then append graph-changing events and finish without any restamp; when A finishes it only clears `_STAMPING`, it does not stamp B’s changes. For example, while an MCP `complete T1` call is restamping, a concurrent `complete T2` call can see `_STAMPING` true, append its completion event, and return, leaving dependents of T2 with stale `wave:*` tags despite `[waves].auto_stamp` being true.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/waves_auto.py:16

chunk_findings.detail: `plan` only emits edits for the items returned by `derive`, and `derive` contains only currently open non-phase items. Therefore a `wave:N` tag on an item that has left the open set is never cleaned. For example, task `T` is open and stamped `wave:0`; then `T` is completed or removed with `[waves].auto_stamp` enabled, or `ddflow waves --stamp` is run. `open_items` drops `T`, `derive` has no entry for `T`, and `plan` produces no edit, so `T` still carries `wave:0` even though its derived wave is “no wave.” A `--check` built from this plan will report the stamp as current while the tag is stale.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waves.py:plan

chunk_findings.detail: A one-node cycle is discarded before cycle detection. `prerequisites` filters dependencies with `d != iid`, so if an open item has itself as a prerequisite (e.g. a hand-edited `needs` edge `A -> A`, or an inherited dependency that resolves to the item itself), `find_cycles` sees no cycle and `derive` gives `A` wave 0. `ddflow waves` then reports a wave and `--stamp` writes `wave:0`, although the stated semantics say cycles get no wave.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/waves.py:prerequisites

chunk_findings.detail: The `waves` command now exposes a mutating option `--stamp` that writes/removes `wave:N` tags, but it is declared as a view family (`family="ddflow_view"`, `help_group="Reading the queue"`). A client or MCP surface that uses the declared family/tool classification to distinguish read-only from mutating tools can call `ddflow_waves` with `stamp=true` and mutate the repo while the command is still declared as a view. This misdeclares the command’s side-effect class in the MCP parity declaration; the stamping path should be declared as a write/update command/tool or the mutating option should be separated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/waves.py (command `waves`, `family="ddflow_view"`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `_waves` helper returns only one `wave:*` tag per non-terminal item (the last matching tag wins), so it cannot prove that a stale wave tag was removed. In `test_a_hand_edit_is_overwritten_and_only_that_item_is_written`, if `--stamp` adds `wave:2` but fails to remove the manually added `wave:9`, and C’s tag list ends with `wave:2`, the assertion `_waves(repo)["C"] == "wave:2"` still passes even though C still has `wave:9`. Thus the test does not actually verify the stated behavior that a hand edit of `wave:*` is overwritten; it should assert the exact set of wave tags, e.g. `{"wave:2"}` for C.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_waves_stamp.py:_waves / test_a_hand_edit_is_overwritten_and_only_that_item_is_written

chunk_findings.detail: The new OK branch assumes `out.data` is a dict and calls `out.data.get(...)` unconditionally. The previous implementation explicitly tolerated `out.exit == O.OK` with falsy/`None` `out.data` and returned `0`. If `batch.apply` returns OK with no payload (for example, a concurrent stamp already applied the edits, or a no-op transaction reports OK with `data=None`), this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'` instead of returning `0`, crashing `ddflow waves --stamp` and any auto-stamp path. The old `out.data` guard should be restored, e.g. `len((out.data or {}).get("edits", []))`.

chunk_findings.detail: The `waves` command now exposes a mutating option `--stamp` that writes/removes `wave:N` tags, but it is declared as a view family (`family="ddflow_view"`, `help_group="Reading the queue"`). A client or MCP surface that uses the declared family/tool classification to distinguish read-only from mutating tools can call `ddflow_waves` with `stamp=true` and mutate the repo while the command is still declared as a view. This misdeclares the command’s side-effect class in the MCP parity declaration; the stamping path should be declared as a write/update command/tool or the mutating option should be separated.

chunk_findings.detail: The `_waves` helper returns only one `wave:*` tag per non-terminal item (the last matching tag wins), so it cannot prove that a stale wave tag was removed. In `test_a_hand_edit_is_overwritten_and_only_that_item_is_written`, if `--stamp` adds `wave:2` but fails to remove the manually added `wave:9`, and C’s tag list ends with `wave:2`, the assertion `_waves(repo)["C"] == "wave:2"` still passes even though C still has `wave:9`. Thus the test does not actually verify the stated behavior that a hand edit of `wave:*` is overwritten; it should assert the exact set of wave tags, e.g. `{"wave:2"}` for C.

chunk_findings.detail: The new OK branch assumes `out.data` is a dict and calls `out.data.get(...)` unconditionally. The previous implementation explicitly tolerated `out.exit == O.OK` with falsy/`None` `out.data` and returned `0`. If `batch.apply` returns OK with no payload (for example, a concurrent stamp already applied the edits, or a no-op transaction reports OK with `data=None`), this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'` instead of returning `0`, crashing `ddflow waves --stamp` and any auto-stamp path. The old `out.data` guard should be restored, e.g. `len((out.data or {}).get("edits", []))`.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard still does not honour `on` after the command body. `keep_stamped` computes `on` and sets `before = None` when `on` is false (auto-stamping disabled, or the re-entrancy guard is active), but the post-command check is only `if log.mark() != before:`. With `[waves].auto_stamp=false`, a wrapped graph-changing command appends an event, `log.mark()` becomes non-`None`, the condition is true, and `waves.restamp` writes/removes `wave:N` tags even though the knob says not to stamp. The same omission defeats the re-entrancy guard: while `_STAMPING` is true, a nested `keep_stamped` gets `before=None` and will also call `restamp` after the nested events, contrary to the stated purpose of the guard.

chunk_findings.detail: The `limit` value is accepted as any integer, but `text` treats it as a slice bound. With `args={"limit": -1}` and a wave containing one item, `report` stores `limit=-1`, then `text` evaluates `ids[:-1]`, which returns an empty list and prints `... 1 more (--limit 0 lists all)`. A negative limit therefore produces incorrect truncation instead of either being rejected or treated as “no limit” like `0`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/waves.py:text

chunk_findings.detail: `_STAMPING` is a process-wide boolean, not a per-command/thread/context-local guard. `keep_stamped` disables itself whenever `_STAMPING` is true (`on = not _STAMPING and bool(cfg.waves.auto_stamp)`), and it sets `_STAMPING = True` for the duration of `waves.restamp(...)`. In an MCP server or any threaded/async host that can have two ddflow commands in flight, a restamp for command A will make an unrelated command B take the `if not on: yield; return` path. B can then append graph-changing events and finish without any restamp; when A finishes it only clears `_STAMPING`, it does not stamp B’s changes. For example, while an MCP `complete T1` call is restamping, a concurrent `complete T2` call can see `_STAMPING` true, append its completion event, and return, leaving dependents of T2 with stale `wave:*` tags despite `[waves].auto_stamp` being true.

chunk_findings.detail: `plan` only emits edits for the items returned by `derive`, and `derive` contains only currently open non-phase items. Therefore a `wave:N` tag on an item that has left the open set is never cleaned. For example, task `T` is open and stamped `wave:0`; then `T` is completed or removed with `[waves].auto_stamp` enabled, or `ddflow waves --stamp` is run. `open_items` drops `T`, `derive` has no entry for `T`, and `plan` produces no edit, so `T` still carries `wave:0` even though its derived wave is “no wave.” A `--check` built from this plan will report the stamp as current while the tag is stale.
